# Dairy food intake is not associated with frailty in adults from the Framingham Heart Study

**Authors:** Anna C. Siefkas; Courtney L. Millar; Alyssa B. Dufour; Douglas P. Kiel; Paul F. Jacques; Marian T. Hannan; Shivani Sahni

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA | 2Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research, Hebrew SeniorLife, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 3Nutritional Epidemiology Program, Jean Mayer, USDA HNRCA, Tufts University, Friedman School of Nutrition, Boston, MA

## Abstract

Nutrients including protein, calcium, and fat may be associated with risk of frailty, yet specific contributions from whole dairy foods rich in these nutrients remain understudied.

To determine associations between dairy intake [milk, yogurt, cheese, total (milk+yogurt+cheese), low-fat, and high-fat dairy, servings/week] and frailty onset and frailty phenotype components.

Prospective cohort study. All dairy intake exposures (servings/week) were assessed via a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ).

Participants (aged 33–86 years) from the Framingham Offspring Study who were not frail at baseline (1998–2001), completed a FFQ and had 1 or 2 follow-up frailty assessments (2005–2008, 2011–14) were included.

Frailty was defined as the presence of ≥3 Fried frailty phenotype components: unintentional weight-loss, exhaustion, slowness (gait speed), weakness (grip strength), and low physical activity. Individuals with 0–2 components were considered non-frail.

Repeated measures logistic regression estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for frailty onset. Logistic (exhaustion and weight loss) and linear regression (gait speed, grip strength, and physical activity) estimated the association between baseline dairy intake and each frailty component at follow-up, adjusting for baseline values for age, sex, energy intake (residual analysis), current smoking, and multivitamin use. Models were further adjusted for health status in a secondary analysis.

Mean baseline age (±SD) was 61 years (±9, range 33–87), and 54% were female. Of 2,550 non-frail individuals at baseline, 8.8% (2005–2008) and 13.5% (2011–2014) became frail. Higher yogurt intake was associated with decreased odds of frailty [OR = 0.96 (95% CI: 0.93–0.99), p = 0.02]. Each additional serving of yogurt [ β (SE): 0.004 (0.001), p < 0.01] and low-fat dairy [ β (SE): 0.001 (0.0006), p = 0.04] was associated with significantly faster follow-up gait speed. Dietary intakes of high-fat dairy were associated with increased odds of frailty [OR = 1.02 (95% CI: 1.00–1.04), p = 0.05], but the p-value was of borderline significance. No associations were observed for other dairy foods. After adjusting for health status, the associations of high-fat dairy and yogurt with frailty became non-significant, although the magnitudes of the associations did not change. The association between yogurt and gait speed decreased in magnitude after adjusting for health status [ β (SE): 0.002 (0.001), p = 0.01].

Dietary intakes of yogurt were modestly associated with reduced frailty onset and dietary intakes of high-fat dairy had a borderline association with increased odds of frailty, but other dairy food intakes showed no association in this study of healthy adults. Some dairy food intakes were modestly associated with follow-up gait speed. However, effect sizes were small, and the clinical importance of these associations remains undetermined.

## Introduction

Frailty is an emerging public health concern given the growing aging population.1 Frailty is generally conceptualized as a syndrome of decreased functional reserve, increased vulnerability to stressors, and loss of physical function characterized by sarcopenia,2 which places older adults at greater risk of falls, fractures, disability, and mortality.2,3 Although the concept of frailty is widely accepted, its causes are multifactorial, and its risk factors are not fully understood. Given the growing numbers of older adults surviving to advanced age across the world,4 an improved understanding of the determinants of frailty is essential to develop novel interventions for prevention and treatment.

Prior research has indicated that diet is strongly linked to frailty risk. Dietary patterns (such as the Mediterranean diet),5 macronutrients (protein),6 micronutrients (e.g., vitamin D, carotenoids), and omega-3 fatty acids7,8 have been associated with frailty risk. Furthermore, undernutrition is frequent among those with frailty.9 Protein is the most studied nutrient in relation to frailty, and prior research has shown that dietary protein could be protective against frailty in longitudinal studies.10,11 However, the impacts of specific high-protein foods such as dairy foods on frailty remain under-studied, despite emerging evidence indicating that protein source, in addition to protein quantity, may affect frailty risk.12–14

Dairy foods are a source of high-quality protein and are also energy dense.15 Small changes in dairy intake may therefore result in large changes in protein and caloric intake, which could protect against the low energy intake and wasting often seen in frailty.16 As a result, dairy foods may provide particularly effective avenues for frailty intervention. Therefore, the objective of the present study was to determine the association between dairy food intake and two frailty-related outcomes: the Fried frailty phenotype and its components. We hypothesized that higher dairy food intake [milk, yogurt, cheese, total dairy (milk+yogurt+cheese), low-fat dairy, and high-fat dairy, servings/week] would be favorably associated with components of the Fried frailty phenotype and lower odds of frailty onset over approximately 11 years of follow-up.

## Methods

### Study Population

Study participants included men and women from the Framingham Heart Study (FHS) Offspring cohort, a prospective cohort study. From 1971–1975, 5,124 offspring of the original FHS participants were enrolled in the Framingham Offspring Study (FOS) to investigate familial risk factors for cardiovascular disease.17 Detailed in-person examinations have been conducted approximately every four years in the FOS.18 The present study was approved by the institutional review board at Hebrew SeniorLife.

The study included FOS participants who completed a frailty assessment at the index exam (1998–2001), completed a diet assessment at the index exam and, optionally, the exam prior (1995–1998), and later completed frailty assessments at follow-up examinations in 2005–2008 and/or in 2011–2014. Participants were only included if they had valid FFQs completed during the index exam (1998–2001); valid dietary information from the prior exam (1995–1998) was included if available. Invalid FFQs were defined as those with >12 food items left blank, or extreme energy intakes of <600 or >4,000 kcal/day (females) and <600 or ≥4,200 kcal/day (males) at the baseline examination. Participants with valid FFQs with complete information on one or more dairy foods were included. Participants who were frail at baseline (i.e., met three or more of the Fried frailty phenotype criteria described under Frailty Measures below) or those individuals whose frailty status could not be determined at the follow-up were excluded. This study population was used for primary analyses of frailty onset and frailty phenotype components.

To address the issue that participants may move in and out of frailty states (e.g., experience a temporary frailty onset followed by a reversal of frailty), a secondary analysis was conducted for frailty onset over a short-term follow-up. Participants free of frailty in 1998–2001 and/or 2005–2008 were included and assessed for the onset of frailty at the next exam (either 2005–2008 or 2011–2014, respectively) resulting in the total number of 4,511 observations for 2,745 study participants that were included in this analysis.

### Dairy food intake

Dietary assessment was conducted in 1995–1998 and 1998–2001 using the validated Harvard 126-item semi-quantitative FFQ.19 Given that milk, calcium, and vitamin D intake have been reported to be fairly stable over 18 years of follow-up20 in other populations, we averaged the dietary intakes across both assessment cycles for the present study. Use of cumulative averages of multiple dietary assessments to represent long-term intake is often used in large epidemiological studies to minimize within-person variation, to alleviate random and systematic measurement errors of FFQ, and to capture chronic dairy exposure.19,21–23 Information on total energy intake and multivitamin supplement use was also evaluated by the FFQ.

Intake of milk, yogurt, cheese, a combination of milk + yogurt + cheese (total dairy), low-fat dairy, and high-fat dairy was estimated in servings per week. Milk intake was calculated as the sum of intake of skim milk, low-fat milk, whole milk, and sherbet/ice milk. Cheese intake was calculated as the sum of intake of cottage/ricotta cheese and other cheeses (e.g. American, Cheddar, etc.). Yogurt intake was defined as consumption of any kind of yogurt and did not include information on addition of sweeteners or low vs high fat. Intake of yogurt drinks was not assessed. Total dairy intake was calculated as the sum of milk + yogurt + cheese. Low-fat dairy food was defined as the sum of intake of skim milk or low-fat milk, sherbet/ice milk and yogurt. High-fat dairy food was defined as the sum of intake of whole milk, ice cream, cottage/ ricotta cheese and other cheese. Harvard’s FFQ specifies the serving size for each dairy food as follows: milk, skim/low-fat/whole (8 oz. glass or 237 mL), ice milk/sherbet (1/2 cup or 118 mL), cottage/ricotta cheese (1/2 cup or 118 g), other cheese (1 slice, 1 oz. serving, or 18 g), ice cream (1/2 cup or 188 g), and yogurt (1 cup or 237 g). According to the definitions by the USDA Food Groups24 and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans,25 milk products with little to no calcium are not included in the dairy group. Therefore, we did not include cream, sour cream, cream cheese, and butter in any of the dairy groups for the present analyses.

### The Onset of Frailty and components of the Fried frailty phenotype

Frailty was assessed at three examination periods (1998–2001, 2005–2008, and 2011–2014) using a modified Fried’s frailty phenotype.2 Individuals were classified as frail if they fulfilled at least three of the following frailty components: unintentional weight loss (4.54 or more kg per year), self-reported exhaustion defined using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression scale,26 weakness (lowest grip strength quintile defined by sex and body mass index [BMI]), slow walking speed (lowest quintile defined by sex and height), and low physical activity (lowest sex-specific quintile). All individuals with fewer than three of these components were considered non-frail. Grip strength and gait speed cut-points were defined as in Fried et al.2

Gait speed (m/s) was measured as the faster of the two walk trials of 4 meters at usual pace. Grip strength (kg) was measured using a Jamar dynamometer (Lafayette Instrument Co, Lafayette, IN) and was recorded as the maximum of six trials (three per hand). 27 Handling of the missing data for frailty has been previously described.28,29 Briefly, those who had missing grip strength and/or gait speed measurements, but who reported physical limitations, were assumed to fulfill the criteria of low grip strength and/or slow gait speed. As has been done in prior work,28,29 we modified two of the criteria to define frailty over 3 examinations such that unintentional weight loss was defined as self-reported unintentional weight loss of more than 4.54 kg in the last year or an annualized weight loss of more than 4.54 kg per year or BMI <18.5 kg/m2. Additionally, physical activity was measured using the Physical Activity Index (PAI).30 Physical activity cut-offs established at the first exam were used at follow-up examinations to classify individuals with low physical activity; PAI scores of 32.6 defined the lowest quintile both for men and women at the first exam.

### Covariates

Covariate information was obtained from measures collected closest to the time of the baseline exam when diet was measured and included sex, age, current smoking, energy intake, multivitamin use. Since frailty tracks with other comorbidities, models were further adjusted for self-reported health status, cognitive status, and indicators of common diseases linked to both diet and frailty [diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and non-skin cancers]. Finally, to assess the impact of socioeconomic status and diet quality on associations between dairy intake and frailty, frailty onset models were further adjusted for education level and Mediterranean-style dietary pattern score (MSDPS) 31 as a measurement of diet quality. Self-reported smoking status over the past year was assessed via questionnaire and participants were categorized as current smoker (yes/no). Energy intake (kcal/d) and multivitamin use (yes/no) was from the FFQ. Health status was self-reported as poor/fair, good, or excellent. Cognitive status was evaluated by the Mini-mental state exam (MMSE),32 for which scores range from 0 – 30 points, with lower scores indicating greater impairment. Persons with a history of diabetes mellitus, who used oral hypoglycemic medications or insulin, or who had a baseline fasting plasma glucose level >126 mg/dL (>7.0 mmol/L) or a baseline post-oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) plasma glucose level >200 mg/dL (>11.1 mmol/L) were categorized as having diabetes. CVD was defined as coronary heart disease (coronary death, myocardial infarction, coronary insufficiency, and angina), cerebrovascular events (including ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and transient ischemic attack) stroke, peripheral artery disease (intermittent claudication) and heart failure. Non-skin cancer was defined as any self-reporting of incident non-skin cancer from previous exam. Diabetes, CVD, and non-skin cancers were modeled using indicator variables to denote the presence or absence of disease. Education level, a marker of socioeconomic status was considered as a covariate and modeled as less than a high school degree, high school degree, some college, or college degree. The MSDPS measures adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet as a proportion of an individual’s total energy intake, and has been described in detail previously.31 The MSDPS was included in models as a numerical score.

### Statistical Analysis

Means and standard deviations were calculated for continuous variables, while percentages were calculated for categorical variables. The primary exposure was energy-adjusted residuals of dairy food intake.33 To determine whether high-fat and low-fat dairy consumption changed over the period of the two visits, mean differences in intake of high- and low-fat dairy between 1995–1998 and in 1998–2001 were assessed, with positive values reflecting increases in intake over time.

The primary analysis examined frailty onset (yes/no) over the long-term study period, while the secondary analysis examined shorter-term frailty onset among participants with frailty information available at sequential study visits. A sensitivity analysis for odds of long-term frailty onset was conducted such that those with missing grip strength or gait speed due to physical limitation were retained as missing those values.

Frailty onset and the phenotype components exhaustion and weight loss were examined as binary outcomes, while gait speed, grip strength, and PAI at follow-up examinations were examined as continuous outcomes in separate models. Before modeling, distributions of continuous dependent variables were examined, and these variables were transformed if they were not normally distributed.

Regression models were used to estimate measures of association and 95% confidence intervals associated with each 1 serving per week higher dairy food intake for milk, cheese, total, high-fat, and low-fat dairy intakes. Because yogurt was log-transformed before modeling, associations with yogurt intake were computed as servings of intake per week on the log scale, i.e., per 2.7 servings per week higher yogurt intake. Logistic regression models were used to calculate odds ratios for all outcomes with the exception of the continuous outcomes of gait speed, grip strength, and PAI, for which linear regression models estimated beta coefficients and P values. For analyses of frailty onset, logistic regression with a repeated measures approach was used. Each dairy intake was analyzed as a separate exposure; only one dairy food was included in each model.

For all analyses, models were initially adjusted for age and sex (Model 1). Subsequent models were further adjusted for energy intake (residual method), current smoking status, and multivitamin use (Model 2) in the primary analysis. In a secondary analysis, Model 2 was further adjusted for health status. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis of the primary frailty onset model (Model 2) was performed where the model was adjusted simultaneously for milk, cheese, and log transformed yogurt to assess the potential for residual confounding by other dairy foods in the primary analysis. We additionally computed models which were further adjusted for MMSE scores and disease indicators for diabetes, CVD, and non-skin cancers (Model 3). Models for components of frailty were further adjusted for baseline values of the components in separate models.

A sensitivity analysis was conducted where such participants with missing grip strength and/or gait speed measurements who reported physical limitation were retained as missing those values and excluded from the analysis. In addition to assessing frailty onset, each frailty component was examined as an independent outcome at the end of follow-up.

A nominal two-sided p value of 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. All analyses were conducted using SAS software version 9.3 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC).

## Results

### Study participants

Of the 5,124 participants enrolled in the Framingham Offspring Study, 3,539 had frailty components assessed at the index exam for this study. After exclusions, 2,524 participants were included in the primary analytic sample (Figure 1). In total, 30 participants who did not complete gait speed testing (n=30) or grip strength testing (n=28) due to physical limitation were considered to fulfill low grip strength or low gait speed criteria, respectively. For models further adjusted for disease indications, 3 participants were excluded due to missing disease indicators.

In this study, 55.5% of the participants were female, the mean age was 60.0 (SD ± 9.0) years (range: 33–86) and mean BMI was 28.0 (SD ± 5.2) (Table 1). Ninety six percent of study participants self-identified themselves as being of European ancestry.34 Mean intake of dairy food groups ranged from 1.0 servings/week for yogurt to 5.7 servings/week for milk; total dairy intake was 9.5 (SD ± 6.4) servings/week (Table 1). Intake of high-fat and low-fat dairy was similar at the two visits from which dairy intakes were averaged. The mean change in intake of high-fat dairy between the 1995–1998 and the 1998–2001 exams was an increase of 1.9 ± 4.6 servings/week, and the mean change in intake of low-fat dairy between these exams was an increase of 0.7 ± 5.3 servings/week. Incidence of frailty at the first follow-up was 8.8% and at the final follow-up examination was 13.5%. Those lost to follow-up (n= 523) were on average older (66.8 ± 9.9 years) and were slightly less likely to be female (51.8% female) than those who remained in the study sample (aged 60.0 years ± 9.0 and 55.5% female). Participants lost to follow-up reported slightly lower mean baseline grip strength (31.3 vs 33.4 kg) and gait speed (1.1 vs 1.2 m/s ) when compared to those who remained in the sample, and were less likely to report excellent health (29% vs 49% ) when compared to the full sample.

### Frailty onset

In the age and sex adjusted models, each 2.7 serving per week higher yogurt intake was associated with a 4% reduction in the odds of long-term frailty onset (Table 2). Each 1 serving per week high-fat dairy food intake was associated with a statistically significant 2% increase in the odds of long-term frailty onset (Table 2). None of the other dairy foods were associated with frailty onset (P range: 0.23 – 0.78). After further adjustment for energy intake, current smoking, and multivitamin use, associations did not change appreciably in magnitude. The association between log-transformed yogurt intake and frailty onset remained statistically significant and the association between high-fat dairy intake and frailty onset became borderline statistically significant (p = 0.05). No other dairy food intakes were significantly associated with onset of frailty (model 2, P range: 0.32 – 0.75). After adjustment for health status, the magnitude of associations did not change, although no associations remained significant (P range: 0.07 – 0.88). The associations of yogurt (0.09) and high-fat dairy (0.07) with frailty continued to trend towards significance after adjustment for health status. Results did not change after further adjustment for disease indicators (data not shown). Additional adjustment for educational attainment and diet-quality as measured by the MSDPS did not change results.

In the sensitivity analysis excluding individuals with missing gait speed and grip strength measures due to physical limitations, results did not meaningfully change when compared to the main analysis. Yogurt intake remained associated with decreased odds of frailty, and high-fat dairy intake with increased odds of frailty (Table 3 [suggested online-only table]). No other dairy food intakes were associated with odds of frailty.

In the secondary analysis of short-term frailty onset, 2,745 participants contributed 4,511 observations to the analysis. Mean follow-up time for those included in analysis of the baseline and first follow-up exam was 6.6 years (± 0.7) years, and mean follow-up time for those included in analysis of the first and second follow-up exams was 5.8 (± 0.6) years. Yogurt intake was associated with 4% lower odds of frailty in the age and sex adjusted models (p = 0.01). The magnitude of the result did not change in Model 2, although statistical significance was attenuated (p = 0.07). No other dairy food intakes were associated with frailty onset in either model (Table 4 [suggested online-only table]). Results did not change after further adjustment (data not shown).

### Fried phenotype components

All continuous component outcomes were normally distributed. When dairy foods were examined for associations with each component of the frailty phenotype at the follow-up examination, no dairy foods were associated with exhaustion or weight loss in the age and sex adjusted models, although point estimates suggested a non-significant increase in the odds of exhaustion for each weekly serving higher of cheese and high-fat dairy (Table 5). Results did not change in Model 2 after adjusting for energy intake, current smoking status, and multivitamin use (Table 5). Results additionally did not change after adjustment for self-reported health status. Further adjustment for disease status did not change these associations (data not shown).

Each 2.7 serving per week higher yogurt intake and each 1 serving per week higher of total dairy intake and low-fat dairy intake were modestly associated with 0.005, 0.001, and 0.002 m/s higher follow-up gait speed, respectively, in the age and sex adjusted models. In Model 2, associations with log-transformed yogurt intake and low-fat dairy intake remained statistically significant, while the association with total dairy intake did not reach significance (p = 0.07) (Table 6). The association between low-fat dairy and gait speed became non-significant (p = 0.1) after adjustment for health status in the secondary analysis, while the association between yogurt and gait speed was attenuated [β (SE): 0.002 (0.001), p = 0.01]. Further adjustment for disease status in Model 3 did not meaningfully alter results. Each 2.7 serving per week higher yogurt intake was also associated with a 0.05-unit higher PAI scores at follow-up when adjusting for age and sex and when adjusting for energy intake, smoking, and multivitamin use, although the association was not statistically significant (p = 0.08) (Table 6). Associations did not change after further adjustment for health status in the secondary analysis, or after adjustment for disease status in Model 3 (data not shown). No dairy foods were associated with follow-up grip strength in any model.

## Discussion

This study demonstrated that dairy food intake is generally not associated with odds of frailty onset over approximately 11 years of follow-up. These results were largely consistent across dairy food categories and robust to sensitivity analysis. In contrast to the overall null results, our results demonstrate that yogurt intake was modestly associated with reduced frailty onset and with presence of frailty phenotype components, and the associations between high-fat dairy intake and frailty onset and between high-fat dairy intake and exhaustion trended towards a deleterious association. However, the effect sizes of these associations were small and may not be clinically meaningful. After adjusting for health status, the magnitude of the relationship between yogurt and gait speed was attenuated; all other estimates of associations maintained the same magnitude, but p-values exceeded the significance threshold of 0.05 after adjusting for health status. Future longitudinal studies should consider the role of health status as a mediator of relationships between dairy intakes and frailty outcomes.

### Onset of Frailty

The limited studies performed to date on the association between dairy intake and frailty onset have been inconclusive.35–37 A recent study of the Three-City Bordeaux cohort of French older adults (mean age 71) reported that no dairy product intakes were associated with frailty prevalence in a cross-sectional analysis. Intake of dairy products (defined as milk, cheese, and fresh dairy products) were similarly not associated with ten-year frailty onset in 823 members of the same cohort.35 In contrast, research in the Seniors-ENRICA cohort has reported that adults over age 60 years and consuming at least 7 servings of low-fat milk or low-fat yogurt a week had a lower risk of incident frailty over 3.5 years when compared to those consuming less than one serving a week (OR = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.29 – 0.90). However, the same study reported that whole milk and cheese intakes were not associated with frailty incidence.36 Another study of 283 older Japanese adults aged 65–86 years reported that increased intake of milk and dairy products (analyzed per SD) was marginally associated with 22% reduced odds of developing pre-frailty or frailty over a two-year period (p = 0.08).37

The failure to demonstrate a general association between dairy intake and frailty onset in the present study may be attributable to several factors. The study population examined in our work was relatively young and healthy, with a mean age of 60 ± 9 years at baseline and a wide age range, while frailty becomes increasingly prevalent with older age.39,40 It is possible that this study population was not sufficiently at risk for frailty for protective associations to be seen, although this possibility is not supported by a similar lack of association between dairy intake and frailty in the older Three-City cohort, where average study participant age was 74 years (±4.9 years).

Across observational studies, variation in results may be in part due to availability and choice of potential confounding variables controlled for in the analysis. Although effort was made to account for overall dietary pattern through the use of the MSDPS, it is also possible that differences in overall diet patterns and diet quality account for differences in findings between studies, given the difficulties that exist in distinguishing the effects of specific dietary components from the effect of overall diet. Differences in findings may also be attributable in part to differences in outcome definitions across studies. However, while the Fried frailty phenotype was modified for use in the present analyses, the same modifications have been used in prior research.28,29

### Frailty phenotype components

Evidence for associations between dairy food intake and frailty phenotype components is limited, although prior research reporting that dietary protein is associated higher grip strength,41 gait speed,42 and muscle quality43 supports the potential impact of dairy protein on frailty phenotype components. A cross-sectional study of 1,456 women aged 70 to 85 years old reported that higher dairy intake (milk, yogurt, and cheese) was associated with higher grip strength and reduced odds of a slow Timed Up and Go test, a measure of functional performance, which incorporates gait speed,44 but data on associations with physical activity are lacking. High consumption of low-fat dairy and low-fat yogurt (≥ 7 servings per week) was also associated with decreased risk of slowness and weight loss over 3.5 years when compared to those consuming less than one serving per week in the Seniors-ENRICA cohort.36 Ricotta cheese intake has also been linked to improvements in muscle mass and reduced loss of grip strength in a randomized controlled trial of 132 men and women over age 60.45 However, a recent meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials reported that dairy protein intake was not associated with handgrip strength46 in 435 men and women aged 55 and older from 7 clinical trials (follow-up time 12 weeks – 2 years).

Our results indicated that small increments of low-fat dairy (1 serving higher per week) and yogurt (2.7 servings higher per week) intake are associated with higher gait speed and higher yogurt intake is associated with higher physical activity at follow-up after adjustment for relevant health behaviors and disease status, although the magnitude of the associations are small. These results support the finding from the Seniors-ENRICA cohort reporting beneficial effects of high consumption of low-fat milk and low-fat yogurt.

The processed nature of much of the cheese produced and consumed in the United States47,48 may have had an impact on these findings and may help explain differences between the observed associations between cheese intake and frailty across studies. The favorable effect of yogurt intake may have been driven by its high-protein, low-fat composition. Yogurt, as a fermented food, may also positively impact human health through effects on the human gut microbiome49,50 which in turn may alter frailty risk in older adults,51 although further research is required to determine causality and elucidate possible mechanisms. Taken together, the finding that intake of different types of dairy foods may primarily drive associations with different aspects of the frailty phenotype may contribute to heterogeneity of study findings and to our finding that dairy food intake is not associated with onset of the frailty.

### Strengths and Limitations

Strengths of this study include the large sample size from a community-based prospective cohort study of men and women, and detailed frailty assessments over a long follow-up time of 10–16 years. The study incorporated detailed assessment of several dairy foods including low-fat and high-fat dairy intake. The FOS is well characterized with detailed assessment of confounders and covariates to account for potential confounding, and used the FFQ, which has been validated in this population.

Potential limitations include the use of FFQ, which is subject to recall bias and lacks detailed information on portion sizes and grams of nutrients. However, it effectively ranks individuals based on their typical nutrient intakes. We were unable to distinguish between high- and low-sugar dairy foods in this analysis, which may explain the lack of associations observed between dairy and frailty in this study because high-sugar foods are associated with poorer frailty outcomes.52 We additionally were unable to distinguish between high-fat and low-fat yogurt in our analysis, although previous research has suggested low-fat yogurt may not be protective against frailty when consumed without other dairy foods.36 Furthermore, based on prior studies, the majority of yogurt consumed in this cohort was considered to be low-fat yogurt,53 which could have led to misclassification of yogurt intake. Given that we were unable to account for cheese intake from mixed dishes in the cheese intake variable, the intake of cheese in this study could have been under-estimated. This analysis did not assess how changes in dairy intake over time may have influenced frailty outcomes, which constitutes a further area for future study. Studies focused on the associations between dairy food intake and progression in frailty status will constitute an important area of future research, as calorie- and nutrient-dense dairy foods may be particularly beneficial in patients who experience frailty. Participants lost to follow-up were on average older and perhaps most susceptible to frailty, which limits generalization to relatively healthier older adults. Residual confounding may have occurred despite our attempts to control for several potential confounders for example residual confounding by overall dietary pattern and quality may have influenced our results even after accounting for dietary quality via the MSDPS. Lastly, the results of our study are generalizable primarily to men and women of European ancestry.

### Conclusion

In the context of prior research, the findings of the present study emphasize the need for continued research to determine the impact of specific protein sources, including dairy, on frailty outcomes. Our findings indicate that yogurt intake is modestly associated with lower odds of frailty as well as higher gait speed and physical activity in middle-aged and older adults, while high-fat dairy may have a deleterious impact on odds of frailty onset. However, effect sizes were small and may not be clinically significant, and the impact of dairy intake on overall frailty incidence remains unclear. In conclusion, dairy food intake is not associated with frailty onset over approximately 11 years of follow-up time in this study of healthy older men and women but may be associated with higher gait speed.
